comment.value: The paper proposes a cache-based acceleration framework for diffusion transformers that reuses intermediate features and applies lightweight learned linear modulation only when necessary, achieving up to 3× FLOP reduction and 2× latency drop on DiT-XL/2, PixArt-α, SD3-medium, and Sana-0.6B while preserving generation quality. Reviewers agree the method is technically solid, easy to plug in, and backed by extensive experiments, but note the linear modulator’s limited expressiveness, sensitivity to the gating threshold, and extra training/tuning burden. Authors adequately addressed these concerns in rebuttal and committed to clarifying the method section and adding ablations. Based on the above reason, this paper is recommended for acceptance.

We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. They found our method to be practical and easy to integrate (aP9D), with strong generalizability and utility across models and tasks (T1S7). Reviewers highlighted the significance of our contribution in substantially reducing FLOPs and inference latency—up to 2.9×—while preserving generation quality across diffusion transformers (T1S7). They also appreciated the novelty of our linear modulation approach, which goes beyond the traditional choice between caching and full inference (3Fgr). The experiments were regarded as comprehensive and solid (aP9D, 3Fgr), and the paper was consistently described as well-written and clearly structured (3Fgr, T1S7). While the reviewers retained their initial scores, they acknowledged that our responses addressed their concerns, and no further questions were raised. We hope this reflects that the main concerns were resolved and that the work’s contributions were appreciated.

rebuttal.value:
We greatly appreciate the insightful comments. Please find our responses to the comments below.

**Q1**. We further explored lightweight nonlinear modulators based on common activation functions such as SiLU [1], sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent (tanh) and softplus. Details of the modulator formulations are found in Table A, where x denotes the cached feature and a and b are trainable scalar parameters. We trained a and b under similar setups to the proposed linear modulator (Appendix A.1). For evaluation, we used the configuration from Table 1: DiT-XL/2 [2] with a 50-step DDIM sampler [3] and an activation cycle $\mathcal{N}=3$, comparing performance of linear and nonlinear modulators. Table B reports 50K image generation performance on ImageNet-1K classes. All linear and nonlinear modulators outperformed the naive caching baseline (FORA [4]), which applies no modulation. However, we observed some variation across different nonlinear function types. Among them, the SiLU-based modulator achieved performance comparable to the proposed linear variant. These results indicate that the effectiveness of nonlinear modulation depends on the choice of function, supporting our use of a simple yet effective linear design with lower computational overhead. Although we experimented with diverse combinations (e.g., initialization, learning rate, threshold, and training iteration) for each nonlinear modulator and reported the best result, further hyperparameter tuning could potentially yield better performance. We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion and will incorporate these experiments into the final version of the paper.

[Table A]
| Method      | Pseudo Code                                                 |
| --------  | ---------------------------------------------------- | 
| linear    | a * x + b                                            |
| SiLU  | a * silu(x) + b                                    | 
| softgate  | sigmoid(a*x+b) * x                                   |
| tanh      | a * tanh(x) + b                                      |
| softplus&log   | log(clamp((softplus(a) + eps) * x, min=eps, max=1e4)) + b | 

※ eps = 1e-6

---
[Table B]


| Method                        | FID↓   | sFID↓  | IS↑      | Precision↑ | Recall↑ |
|-------------------------------|-------:|-------:|---------:|-----------:|--------:|
| DiT-XL/2 (50 steps, baseline) | 2.29  | 4.32  | 239.54  | 0.81      | 0.60   |
| FORA (no modulatiors)          | 3.28  | 5.72  | 228.47  | 0.80      | 0.56   |
| Ours (linear)                 | 2.90  | 4.60  | 231.54  | 0.80      | 0.58   |
| SiLU                      | 2.99  | 4.74  | 230.22  | 0.79      | 0.58   |
| softgate                      | 3.00  | 4.78  | 231.93  | 0.80      | 0.57   |
| tanh                          | 3.13  | 4.66  | 226.21  | 0.79      | 0.58   |
| softplus&log                       | 3.25  | 5.73  | 229.53  | 0.80      | 0.56   |


---

**Q2. (Model distillation)** The proposed framework does not require updating network weights; instead, only the modulators and routers are trained, making it generally applicable to model distillation. However, as discussed in Appendix B.5, its effectiveness may be limited in scenarios where feature similarity between adjacent timesteps is low—such as the latent consistency model [5] we tested.

**(Low-precision)** We validate the effectiveness of our framework under a low-precision setting (8-bit weights, 16-bit activations), using DiT-XL/2 [2] with a 50-step DDIM sampler [3], activation cycle $\mathcal{N}=3$ and a modulation gate threshold of 0.90. To obtain FP8 weights, we apply basic channel-wise symmetric quantization. Following the setup in Table 1, we evaluate performance on the 50K ImageNet 1K-class generation task. As shown in the table below, compared to DDIM 50%-steps with similar generation quality, our method requires 1.46× fewer FLOPs. Moreover, compared to FORA [4] and DDIM with 36% of the steps (which incur similar FLOPs), our method achieves better image quality. These results demonstrate that our method remains effective even under low-precision settings, not just in full-precision (32-bit) scenarios. We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestion and will include the corresponding experiments in the final version of the paper.

|--------------------------------|-----------:|-------:|-------:|---------:|-----------:|--------:|
| DiT-XL/2   (50steps, baseline) | 11.44     | 2.46  | 4.70  | 237.76  | 0.80      | 0.60   |
| 50% steps                      | 5.72      | 3.18  | 5.30  | 231.12  | 0.79      | 0.58   |
| 36% steps                      | 4.12      | 4.37  | 6.43  | 214.37  | 0.77      | 0.56   |

| Ours   ($\mathcal{N}=3$)        | 3.91      | 3.22  | 5.13  | 224.87  | 0.79      | 0.57   |

[2] Peebles, W. & Xie., S. Scalable diffusion models with transformers. In ICCV, 2023

[3] Song, Ji., et al. Denoising diffusion implicit models. In ICLR, 2021

We truly appreciate the constructive suggestions. We provide responses to each comment below. 


**Q1**. While FasterCache [1] also utilizes modulation mechanism, it combines two recently cached features using a deterministic weighting function that is adaptively adjusted by timestep. In contrast, our method relies on only a single cached feature for modulation. Also, FasterCache differs in its application of classifier-free guidance, where it caches the high- and low-frequency biases between conditional and unconditional outputs using Fourier transformation—an approach not adopted in our framework. Overall, while our method requires training a lightweight modulator, it remains more efficient than FasterCache in terms of memory at runtime inference. In the final version, we will properly cite [1] in the related work section, and clearly articulate the differences in motivation and design between our method and theirs. 

---

**W4**. We agree that modulators introduce some overhead. However, heuristic approaches like ToCa [2] also require careful hyperparameter tuning, as they rely on multiple criteria to decide which feature to cache. 

---

**W5**. The proposed framework aims to approximate full diffusion transformer computation through caching and selective modulation for efficient inference. To minimize inference overhead introduced by the modulators, we adopt lightweight linear transformations. Since the modulation is applied to features that are already the outputs of attention and MLP layers, we chose not to use additional MLP- or attention-based modulators. 

---

**References**

[1] Lv, Z., et al. FasterCache: Training-free video diffusion model acceleration with high quality. In ICLR, 2025

[2] Zou, C., et al. Accelerating diffusion transformers with token-wise feature caching. In ICLR, 2025

We sincerely appreciate the thoughtful feedback. We address the comments below.

**W1&W2.** Our framework aims for efficient inference by approximating full diffusion transformer computation through caching and lightweight modulation, leveraging the strong linear relationship between features at consecutive timesteps. As noted in Line 136, the naive caching mechanism alone provides decent generative performance, so we introduce a modulation gate to selectively apply modulation. We adopt a linear modulator based on the observed linear relationship, and deliberately keep it lightweight to maintain efficiency, which naturally limits its expressiveness. As a result, excessive application has been observed to degrade generative performance (Line 229). However, as shown in Figure 5, in the range $[0.90, 0.93]$ close to the reported threshold of 0.9, the FID metric varies by no more than 0.1 across activation cycles of 2, 3 and 5, suggesting that the performance remains reasonably consistent under different threshold settings. We also thank the reviewer for pointing out the clarity issue in the method section. In the final version, we plan to improve accessibility by adding a clearer high-level description and enhancing the illustrations.

summary.value:
The paper introduces a selective caching framework that speeds up diffusion transformers by recycling intermediate features that look alike across neighboring timesteps. When a cached activation is sufficiently close to what the network would recompute, the model skips the full block and, at most, applies a learned scale-and-shift modulation. A tiny gate, trained with the rest of the transformer frozen, decides when this lightweight adjustment is needed. Because fewer than two percent of blocks receive modulation, the extra operations are almost free, and the approach can be inserted into existing samplers without architectural changes.

Tests on several diffusion transformers confirm the efficiency gains. With DiT-XL/2 the method cuts FLOP by about 3× and wall clock time by 2×, yet keeps FID, sFID, and IS comparable. Similar savings are observed on PixArt-α, SD3-medium, and Sana-0.6B, including high-resolution 1024 × 1024 synthesis. Across these models it consistently surpasses prior caching techniques such as FORA and ToCa, and it outperforms simple step-reduction baselines at matched compute budgets.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength:
1. Across four backbones the cache scheme cuts floating point operations and wall clock time, yet FID, sFID, and IS stay comparable of the original samplers at all tested resolutions.
2.  This method is easy to integrate. Only a light gating head is trained while the diffusion transformer stays frozen, so existing checkpoints can adopt the method without any retraining of the large backbone.
3. The experiments are comprehensive and solid. The authors evaluate DiT-XL/2, PixArt-α, SD3-medium, and Sana-0.6B at 256, 512, and 1024 pixel outputs, report both FLOPs and wall clock time, and run ablations on cache depth, gate threshold, and modulation cost. Results are matched to the compute budget of ToCa, FORA, and step-reduction baselines, which makes the gains in speed and quality easy to verify.

Weakness:
1. The method section could be made more accessible.
2. The ablation study uncovers a counter-intuitive trend: when the gate threshold is set low and many blocks are modulated, FID actually increases and image quality drops. This unexpected behaviour shows that the method is sensitive to the threshold and that excessive modulation can harm, rather than help, performance.

summary.value: The paper proposes a cache-based framework for diffusion transformers that improves inference efficiency by reusing features and selectively modulating them through learned linear transformations, achieving comparable generation quality with significantly reduced computational cost.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. The manuscript is well-written, exhibiting a clear and coherent structure that facilitates comprehension.
2. Comprehensive and effective experiments: The method is validated across multiple models and datasets, outperforming SOTA caching methods like FORA and ToCa with comparable or lower computational cost.
3. Building on existing feature caching methods, the paper introduces a novel linear modulation scheme that goes beyond the traditional choice between caching and full inference, enabling more flexible feature reuse.
Weakness:
1. Increased pipeline complexity: Although the training overhead is small, the introduction of modulators and gating mechanisms adds extra training and threshold tuning compared to the heuristic caching method.
2. Limited modulation capacity? Applying modulation to all layers degrades quality, possibly due to the limited expressiveness of linear transformations. Could stronger modulators like MLPs or attention improve performance in more complex scenarios

title.value: Diffusion on Demand: Selective Caching and Modulation for Efficient Generation

abstract.value: Diffusion transformers demonstrate significant potential for various generation tasks but are challenged by high computational cost. Recently, feature caching methods have been introduced to improve inference efficiency by storing features at certain timesteps and reusing them at subsequent timesteps. However, their effectiveness is limited as they rely only on choosing between cached features and performing model inference. Motivated by high cosine similarity between features across consecutive timesteps, we propose a cache-based framework that reuses features and selectively adapts them through linear modulation. In our framework, the selection is performed via a modulation gate, and both the gate and modulation parameters are learned. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves similar generation performance to the original sampler while requiring significantly less computation. For example, FLOPs and inference latency are reduced by $2.93\times$ and $2.15\times$ for DiT-XL/2 and by $2.83\times$ and $1.50\times$ for PixArt-$\alpha$, respectively. We find that modulation is effective when applied to as little as 2\% of layers, resulting in negligible computation overhead.
